Bittensor’s Subsidy Test

State of Bittensor, November 2026. Bittensor overhauled how it funds subnets in 2026 to link emissions more closely to demand, and early commercial traction accelerated sharply even as network subsidies remain larger. We examine what five teams are building, how paid usage is growing, and how effectively customer payments reach their tokens.

Key Takeaways

In February we called Bittensor the Intelligence Olympics: 128 subnets competing for a fixed pot of new TAO. Since then the network has rewritten how that prize money works. Emissions now follow sustained demand for each subnet’s token, teams below a bar see their share fade, and customers can pay in a way that burns tokens at the point of sale.

This report asks one question: are customers starting to pay for what the subsidy built? Increasingly, yes. Estimated customer revenue roughly doubled from ~$35M in August to ~$70M in November, showing clear commercial momentum even while a gap remains beside ~$243M in annual TAO issuance. Outside Lium, matched on-chain buybacks still hold near 5% of minted TAO, yet if this upward revenue trend continues and broadens, the outlook for the network is genuinely encouraging.

New to Bittensor?

Bittensor is a network of specialized markets called subnets. Miners provide work, and validators assess it under each subnet’s rules. TAO is the network token; alpha is a subnet’s own token. Emissions are newly issued tokens that help fund participation. Daily TAO emissions are injected into each subnet’s liquidity pool (and fund protocol alpha buys) based on its emission share, while subnet owners, validators and miners are paid in liquid alpha. A halving reduces the issuance rate. Customer revenue is separate: it comes from people paying for a service. Customer payments can create demand for alpha through mechanisms such as buybacks and burns.

About this joint report

This report is a joint research effort by Khala Research and Subnet Summer, combining Khala’s research and editorial analysis with Subnet Summer’s on-chain ecosystem tracking, subnet case-study sourcing and empirical buyback analysis (Table 11). See About Subnet Summer and Disclosures for full background and affiliations.

01 · Bittensor in 2026

The network changed who gets paid

In short. The 2026 rules tied each subnet’s emissions to demand for its token. Estimated customer revenue has risen, though emissions still fund most of the network’s early-stage buildout.

Every early-stage AI business runs on someone’s subsidy. Centralized frontier labs burn tens of billions in private venture capital to fund research and subsidize inference while chasing scale, whereas Bittensor, carrying a $3.89B fully diluted valuation at $185 per TAO on November 26, uses roughly $243M a year in gross issuance as an open-market venture fund anyone can compete for.

Unlike private venture losses that fall on LPs who signed up for them, token emissions dilute every holder. Under early dTAO, teams could collect emissions whether paying customers showed up or not, so 2026 became Bittensor’s shift from an open-ended subsidy to a performance-gated venture market, testing whether decentralized AI teams can build businesses that outgrow their own subsidies.

Institutional access widened alongside those rule changes, though regulated vehicles remain modest beside daily issuance. In February we pointed to early entry through Grayscale, European ETPs and DCG-backed Yuma.

  • U.S. trust and ETF filing: The Grayscale Bittensor Trust (GTAO) held $17.73M in net assets at September 30, up from $7.97M at year-end 2025, and filed Amendment No. 2 to Form S-1 on October 23 seeking NYSE Arca spot ETF conversion.
  • European ETPs and subnet funds: Regulated staked wrappers such as Deutsche Digital Assets and Safello on SIX and Yuma’s institutional subnet funds broadened non-native access.

Regulated wrappers broaden who can own TAO, which raises the bar for what sits underneath: institutional allocators underwriting the network eventually compare real customer demand against protocol issuance.

Turning subsidized work into a paying business takes different amounts of time across markets. An inference provider can start billing as soon as its API works. A drug-discovery team may spend years testing candidates before a pharmaceutical company licenses one. Both need funding while they build, and both compete for the network’s emissions.

Two pressures forced the 2026 overhaul after our February report:

  • Self-gaming under TaoFlow: Because daily TAO issuance is fixed, a team could bid up its own token to lift its emission share without paying customers, while root stakers earned yield without choosing which subnets to back.
  • Team retention risk: On April 9, 2026, Covenant AI, the team behind Templar SN3, Basilica SN39 and Grail SN81, exited Bittensor after completing its 72B pre-training run, turning long-term alignment into a network-wide concern.

July’s reforms were built to tie emissions to sustained token price share rather than short-term flows. The 2026 upgrades tackled three questions in turn:

  • Who deserves the subsidy: The Emission Gate and Root Reborn tie protocol funding to sustained token demand rather than short-term trading volume.
  • Who gets paid inside each subnet: eTAO lets subnet owners tune weekly splits between owners, validators and miners.
  • How customer cash reaches the token: Gamma links customer billing directly to alpha burns at the point of sale.

The July reforms

July’s reforms linked emissions more closely to token price. The Emission Gate reduces a subnet’s allocation when its share of total subnet token prices falls below a threshold. Root Reborn changed what network-wide stakers earn. Their yield now comes from baskets of subnet tokens chosen by validators.

That choice matters because nearly half of all TAO still sits in root: 5.4 million TAO, or 48%, on July 24, and 5.56 million of 11.76 million TAO, or 47.3%, on November 26. Root’s share stayed virtually flat after Root Reborn.

Stakers can still delegate to a validator, but the subnet tokens inside that validator’s basket now directly shape their yield.

A first way to bet against a subnet

Three follow-on releases extended July’s reforms through the fall:

  • October · eTAO: Shifted attention inside each subnet by letting owners adjust weekly how emissions split across the owner at 0% to 33%, validators up to 50%, and miners at least 33%. Some teams cut their own share to 0% as a commitment signal, while others raised it toward R&D and lab costs.
  • November 9 · Gamma: Links customer billing to the token market at the point of sale through dollar-valued service credits minted via alpha burns. By November 26, 18 subnets had enabled Gamma, with $104K minted and $75.8K spent across the network, led by Lium at $80.3K minted.
  • November 23 · Gate expansion: Two weeks later, on November 23, the OpenTensor Foundation adjusted the gate itself, raising the subnet cap from 128 to 160 and widening the Emission Gate cutoff from rank 32 to rank 48 to open 32 new slots and let more teams earn meaningful emissions. Because the gate’s price-share threshold (θ) is calibrated to that target rank cutoff, moving it to rank 48 lowers θ so subnets ranked 33 through 48 receive meaningful rewards while keeping the steep fade-off for teams below the bar.

What changed in practice

The first visible result was emission concentration. In July’s simulation, the gate lifted the top eight subnets’ share from 32.8% to 52.7%. Live readings reached 57.0% on November 10 before easing to 51.7% on November 26 after the cutoff widened to rank 48, led by Lium at 15.76% and Chutes at 7.94%.

Because daily live tracking begins after July’s upgrade, those figures show how concentrated emissions are today rather than proving the exact share the gate caused.

SubConnect’s annualized index estimate rose from ~$35M in August to ~$70M in November. Part of that jump reflects how the index is compiled: it expanded coverage, moved from heavier extrapolation in early October to direct team check-ins in November, and annualizes trailing monthly or hourly run rates, which can overstate full-year revenue when usage fluctuates. The upgrades’ contribution is unproven.

A live on-chain check: SubConnect’s Bittensor Revenue Index dashboard

Alongside its monthly check-in index, SubConnect launched a live on-chain dashboard at bittensorrevenueindex.com, updated hourly across all 128 subnets. Rather than off-chain invoices, it counts alpha buybacks, Gamma mints and miner registration fees, excluding protocol chain buys.

Three points separate the headline from what actually enters subnets on-chain (full breakdown in Box 1):

  • Different metrics: The dashboard’s $71.98M 30-day annualized headline as of November 25 measures on-chain inflows, not off-chain revenue, so it should not be read as confirming the ~$70M monthly index.
  • 30% headline vs. 17.8% matched: November inflows hit $5.02M, or 30% of the 83,840 net TAO minted. Nearly a third of buybacks sits in provisional Tier 4 burns with no matching purchase, and 12% is miner registration fees; strip both out and matched-purchase buybacks come to $3.00M, or 17.8% of minted TAO.
  • Extreme concentration: Lium alone drives 61% of November’s $5.02M total.

The Lium question

Figure 3 exposes the central tension of Bittensor’s late-2026 numbers. Strip out one GPU-rental subnet, Lium (SN51), and November looks identical to the flat ten months before it: roughly 5.4% matched buybacks and 11.5% total inflows.

Reconciling Lium’s buybacks with its fee revenue
Implied monthly fees~$116K / mo5% fee on Oct’s $2.32M GPU rentals (~$1.39M/yr)
Matched buy-and-burn$2.08MVisibly bought on-chain & burned in Nov (~18× monthly fees)
Nov headline total$3.08M61% of network inflows; adds $995K burned with no matching purchase

Even after stripping out $995K of alpha burned with no matching on-chain purchase (Tier 4 in Box 1), Lium still bought and burned more alpha in November alone than a full year of its implied 5% platform fees. Public data cannot yet tell which of three things drove the gap:

  • Built-up reserves: fee revenue accumulated in earlier months and deployed in November.
  • A November demand surge: GPU rental volume jumping well above October’s $2.32M pace.
  • Gross rental pass-through: gross customer spend flowing through buybacks rather than net 5% fees.

Until an audit clarifies the source, November’s spike should not be assumed as steady-state fee cash flow.

Context: Lium also receives 15.76% of network emissions (~$38.3M/yr at $185/TAO). The $2.08M matched buy-and-burn total (Tier 1 in Box 1) includes $80.1K in Gamma mints, of which $36K came from other subnets’ emissions.

On-chain buybacks also remain highly concentrated. Across all 128 subnets, the top five drove 92% of November buybacks, and the top ten drove 97%, led by Lium at $3.08M, Vanta at $514.7K, Engy at $186.6K, Almanac at $143.4K and SayGM at $128.0K.

SubConnect’s Audits page also notes that formal off-chain verification is not open yet. On-chain trackers can prove whether alpha was bought, locked or burned, not independently verify how much came from outside customer cash versus treasury reserves or recycled emissions.

Revenue against what the network pays out

The network pays subnets in two forms:

  • New $TAO to liquidity pools: At $185 per TAO on November 26, a year of gross issuance at ~3,600 TAO a day is worth roughly $243M, or 3.5 times SubConnect’s ~$70M revenue estimate. At mid-October’s $275 price, that same issuance equals ~$361M, or 5.2 times revenue, so part of the narrower dollar gap comes from a lower TAO price.
  • Alpha emissions to operators: Owners, validators and miners are paid in each subnet’s own token, which has not yet halved. Subnet Summer estimates annualized sellable alpha at ~$535M on November 16 at $195 per TAO, or ~$468M, about 6.7 times revenue, repriced to November 26. Because many recipients stake or hold, sellable alpha is an upper bound rather than measured selling.

Neither ratio is a break-even target. Like venture-backed AI labs, subnets spend ahead of revenue during their build phase, though emissions dilute every token holder rather than a single cap table.

Figure 3 keeps that trajectory grounded in TAO terms:

  • Flat Jan–Oct baseline: Matched-purchase buybacks held between 1.3% and 9.6% of minted TAO, averaging 5.4% across ten months, while total inflows averaged 11.1%. December 2025’s 1.5% sits on a larger pre-halving denominator.
  • A one-subnet November surge: November’s jump to 17.8% matched and 29.8% total is driven by Lium. Excluding Lium’s $3.08M puts the rest of the network near 5.4% matched and 11.5% total, matching the ten-month average.
  • Closing the gap: Box 2 illustrates how long different monthly growth rates take to match gross issuance and sellable alpha.

Customer spending therefore matters to the network’s long-term economics. Some subnets sell services customers already use; others run research that needs years to reach a market.

Protocol release notes and TAO supply

Conviction. Locking a subnet’s alpha builds conviction over time. Once the subnet is at least a year old, ownership can transfer if the highest-conviction hotkey exceeds 18% of the subnet’s eligible alpha. Protocol rules.

Emission Gate mechanics. The gate scales emissions using s³ ÷ (s³ + θ³), where s is the subnet’s smoothed price share after the miner-burn penalty and θ is the threshold, recalculated every 360 blocks. At the threshold a subnet keeps half its linear share. Root can adjust the threshold.

Illustrative curve. The shaded area is below the threshold.

02 · Categories and Subnets

Five builders at five stages

In short. Five builders, five rungs on the commercial ladder: Carbon and Metanova are still proving their research, REAX has paying users without a token route, Vanta runs buybacks without disclosing the customer-fee share, and Engy converts billed developer usage cleanly into token burns.

These businesses are developing under the same network rules, but their customers and commercial timelines differ.

Different business models, different milestones

Research and commercial services run on different clocks, so judging every subnet by quarterly API revenue misses how early-stage R&D actually advances. For an inference product like Engy, repeat customer orders show whether developers value the service. For a drug-discovery network like Metanova or a physics-validation subnet like Carbon, the near-term milestone is lab or engineering proof an independent partner can reproduce.

The five profiles below walk across that spectrum: starting with Metanova and Carbon as research subnets proving their scientific and engineering evidence, moving through compute and paid inference with Chutes and Engy, and finishing with Vanta and REAX as application-layer products testing how live customer demand reaches alpha.

What Carbon is building

Hardware teams designing batteries, electric motors, chip cooling systems and silicon photonics rely on heavy physics simulations that can take hours per design iteration. Fast AI surrogate models can cut those runtimes from hours to seconds, yet engineers rarely deploy a model they cannot verify: a surrogate that looks accurate on training benchmarks can quietly violate physical laws or break down outside familiar operating conditions.

Carbon is building a validation and discovery layer aimed squarely at that trust gap, targeting engineering teams of 10 to 50 people. Its documentation outlines two commercial services:

  • Evidence Audit. A team supplies an existing fast model along with its operating conditions and reference data; Carbon tests the model and maps out where predictions hold up, where they fail, and where additional simulations or lab experiments are still required.
  • Model Discovery. A customer defines accuracy targets and posts a reward, opening a sponsored challenge for the network to produce a better-performing surrogate model that only qualifies for payout once independently verified.

How the verification works and where Carbon stands

To prevent miners from overfitting black-box checkpoints, Carbon does not grade pre-trained weights. Miners submit reproducible construction recipes, which validators rebuild in a controlled environment, check for physical constraints, and score against hidden benchmark data.

Keeping the model producer outside the grading loop separates Carbon from integrated suites like Ansys SimAI, which train and run predictive models inside one closed platform.

Carbon begins with battery modeling before expanding into chip cooling, electric motors and silicon photonics. Following its November 14 mainnet launch, the team claimed the subnet surpassed the best published motor model within three days, a result not yet independently verified. Even with the testing infrastructure running, we found no public disclosure of a customer paying for either an Evidence Audit or a Model Discovery challenge.

Response to the 2026 rules

Carbon registered on October 4, after the Emission Gate was already live, and operates on the default 18 / 41 / 41 eTAO split. Sitting at rank #86 by market cap and #122 by emission on November 26, it still received 0.00% of network TAO issuance to its pool while alpha emissions continued, illustrating how difficult it is for a newly launched research subnet to earn TAO pool liquidity before demonstrating commercial demand.

How value reaches alpha

Carbon’s investor documentation states that company revenue from Evidence Audits and Model Discovery will fund buybacks and burns of SN116 alpha. Until a first paid engagement closes and flows through that mechanism, the token link remains a plan on paper. On-chain conviction locks remained at 0.0% less than two weeks after mainnet launch but leaves long-term alignment to be built.

Risk Factors
  • Project-based vs. recurring revenue. A single Evidence Audit can answer a narrow engineering question, so sustaining commercial demand requires repeat engagements or ongoing Model Discovery budgets rather than one-off checks.
  • Cold-start pressure and thin independent coverage. Receiving 0.00% of network TAO issuance below the Emission Gate limits protocol support while Carbon hunts for its first paying customers, even after the November 23 widening of the bar to rank 48. Because the subnet is newly launched, independent third-party evaluation also remains sparse, with several of the more detailed external summaries coming from automated news roundups or a third-party report that discloses a conflict of interest.
Takeaway

Carbon’s testing mechanism runs. A first paid audit or settled challenge would show that engineering teams value its evidence enough to pay for it.

What to prove next

Disclose a paid audit with a clear use case and outcome, or a customer-funded discovery challenge with a settled reward. A repeat engagement would help establish recurring demand.

What Metanova is building

Finding a viable drug candidate begins as an enormous search problem: screening billions of chemical structures to locate a few that bind cleanly to a disease target without breaking down too quickly or hitting unintended proteins. Traditional pharmaceutical firms and closed AI labs such as Isomorphic Labs run that work privately behind corporate walls, signing pharma partnerships reported at over $3B.

Metanova makes the opposite bet on SN68. Instead of relying on a single internal research team, it runs continuous open competitions where independent miners compete across three tracks:

  • Small molecules: Conventional chemical compounds proposed and ranked against real disease targets.
  • Chemical-search algorithms: Faster methods to navigate massive chemical libraries without brute-force screening.
  • Nanobodies: Compact single-domain antibodies extending the subnet from small molecules into biologics.

Since launching with single-target screening, the team reports expanding the search space to 678.5 billion possible molecules. Validators score submissions with Boltz-2 and enforce a four-target rule so miners cannot overfit to a single test.

Alongside the subnet, Metanova launched the NOVA Hit-to-Lead Optimization Agent with Chutes and ONEPOT.AI to analyze sensitive molecular data inside a Trusted Execution Environment, according to the team.

“Confidentiality is a central design requirement. Pharmaceutical R&D involves valuable intellectual property, including compound structures, targets, emerging chemical series and optimization strategies that cannot be exposed publicly.”

From software screening to wet-lab testing

Computational rankings only matter once physical compounds are synthesized and tested. Since our February report, SN68’s outputs have begun crossing from digital screening into partner wet labs:

  • Small molecules: A May partnership with ONEPOT.AI gave winning candidates a path to robotic synthesis within days. At October’s Exploit Summit, Metanova reported that most miner-inspired compounds showed a longer test half-life than recently FDA-approved benchmarks.
  • Nanobodies: Yalotein began producing candidates in July, with 50 nanobodies slated for in-vitro testing.

That progress still sits early in a long pipeline: half-life measures chemical stability, not therapeutic safety or efficacy, and no compound has reached lead optimization or preclinical trials yet. Unlike genomics subnets such as Niome and Minos, Metanova’s business depends on patenting assets and licensing them to pharma partners.

Show milestone table and closed-lab comparison (Tables 5 and 6)
Response to the 2026 rules

Metanova cut its miner burn to 0% on June 24, explicitly citing the new incentives: under price-based emissions, burning miner emissions lowers the price share that determines a subnet’s rewards. Under eTAO, the team plans a 26% owner / 41% validator / 33% miner split, directing the larger owner share toward experimental lab data. The practical test is what reproducible wet-lab results that budget produces.

How value reaches alpha

Metanova lists patent licensing, co-development and paid access to its discovery platform as potential sources of commercial revenue. As of mid-October, however, Metanova remained its own first customer, and its public materials disclose neither an outside licensing deal nor a binding policy for routing future licensing proceeds back to SN68 alpha.

Token alignment also needs clarification. On-chain data shows 18.7% of eligible alpha locked and directed to Metanova’s owner hotkey, split across 400K perpetual and 83K decaying alpha, but 0.0% originating from the owner’s wallet itself. While the headline total clears the 18% gate, it only proves team commitment if Metanova controls those separate wallets, a point the team has not yet confirmed publicly.

Risk Factors
  • Biotech timelines and attrition. Drug development routinely takes years, and the vast majority of early-stage candidates fail before reaching a clinic; strong virtual screening scores and initial half-life readouts do not establish therapeutic efficacy.
  • Commercial and token-link lag. Even if partner labs validate a candidate, negotiating pharma licensing deals takes time, and without a documented mechanism tying commercial revenue to SN68 alpha, token holders face open-ended dilution risk. Search metrics are team-reported, and owner-lock totals differ across third-party trackers.
Takeaway

Metanova has moved from computer-based screening into partner lab testing, with early lab results in hand. Its value to alpha holders depends on a licensing route that has not yet been disclosed.

What to prove next

Validate a candidate for its intended use, secure a licensing deal, and disclose how proceeds reach SN68.

Rung 3 of 5 · Paying customers, no route to alpha yetREAX clears the commercial hurdle Carbon and Metanova still face, with paying API users and a #1 benchmark debut, but customer cash does not yet buy back its token.

REAX is one of the newest subnets in this report, live on mainnet only since October 14, 2026. It builds models that choose between a defined set of options, and reports paying customers since launch.

What REAX is building

A support agent could use REAX to decide whether to answer a request, send it to a specialist or hand it to a person. A general-purpose LLM answers in open text. A decision model returns a probability for each option, for example 0.82 answer, 0.15 specialist, 0.03 person.

Software can act on those numbers directly. It can set rules such as handing anything below 0.70 to a person, without parsing a reply or guessing how confident the model is.

Because the task is narrow, REAX’s models stay small, fast and easy for validators to verify:

  • Pricing and verification: On Decision Models, the s1-fast peer-to-peer tier starts at $0.032 per 1M input tokens, while fixed probability outputs let validators recompute answers roughly every two minutes to check fidelity, speed and capacity.
  • API compatibility and early integrations: Compatible with TypeSafe’s Jev service, REAX now supports image-based decisions and, according to the team, powers Trishool’s HaloGuard security product, targeting high-volume routing and guardrail checks in front of frontier LLMs.
  • Hugging Face breakthrough and live usage: On November 6, open-weights REAX 1.3 debuted at #1 of 275 models on the Hugging Face Jev Decision Index at 73.98, ahead of GLiDE 27B at 73.37 and TypeSafe’s closed Jev 1.14 at 60.24. After a November 12 revision and newer entries, it ranked #4 of 346 models at 72.64 on November 26, still 12.4 points above Jev 1.14. REAX reports paying customers since launch, including one making 1.7M weekly requests, though dollar revenue remains undisclosed.

Response to the 2026 rules

Live on mainnet only since October 14, 2026, REAX launched directly into the 2026 rulebook rather than retrofitting an older emission design. Under eTAO, it set a 26% owner, 41% validator and 33% miner split on October 30.

Inside the miner bucket, live inference has taken 30% of rewards since November 2, down from 50%, with any unearned portion burned rather than paid to idle capacity. As of November 26, the 20% REAX Engine track remains paused while the 30% Generalist track is open for Round 2.

How value reaches alpha

Not yet through customer revenue, though the subnet is only six weeks past its October 14 mainnet launch. Fiat billing through Decision Models sits outside the chain’s score ledger, and tao.eco records zero revenue-funded buybacks since October 22, so what burns today is unearned miner emission rather than external cash. On-chain conviction locks also remain small at 2.3% of eligible alpha in a decaying owner lock.

Risk Factors
  • Missing token capture and revenue opacity. Scaling fiat API traffic does not automatically accrue to SN92 alpha without a published buyback, burn or Gamma credit policy, and without disclosed dollar revenue investors cannot gauge how much paid demand exists behind the 1.7M weekly request milestone.
  • Crowded classifier market. Lightweight routing and guardrail models compete directly with closed APIs such as TypeSafe’s Jev as well as inexpensive self-hosted open classifiers that enterprise teams can run on their own infrastructure without touching a decentralized network.
Takeaway

REAX shows that rewards can follow customer demand inside a subnet. For alpha holders, the open question is whether that demand will reach the token.

What to prove next

Disclose recurring paid usage and revenue, then demonstrate a policy and transaction connecting customer payments to alpha.

2.4 Trading: Vanta (SN8)

Rung 4 of 5 · Steady buybacks, unclear customer shareVanta logs on-chain buybacks in 11 of the last 12 months alongside the cohort’s largest owner lock, yet blends evaluation fees with collateral and emissions so customer cash cannot be isolated.

Vanta brings public scoring to trader evaluations

Whereas REAX sells model API calls without token buybacks yet, Vanta already runs recurring buybacks funded from a decentralized prop-trading network where traders pay for evaluations to qualify for capital.

Profile details
Category

Key metric

What Vanta is building

Operated by Taoshi, Vanta runs a decentralized prop-trading network on SN8 across three layers:

  • Protocol scoring: Independent traders, quants and automated models submit live long, short and flat signals across crypto, FX and equities, scored on risk-adjusted returns, drawdowns and consistency.
  • Commercial evaluation funnel: Through Vanta Trading, traders pay cash fees to qualify for funded payouts while prop firms post collateral. The dashboard shows 5,880 cumulative accounts, with 659 active, and the team reports over $1M paid out to 140 traders since April, alongside a new trading workspace, the Glitch AI backtesting tool and a hedge wallet.
  • Market benchmark: Retail prop-trading firms such as FTMO offer the closest benchmark: traders pay upfront to prove they can hit profit targets without breaching drawdown limits. FTMO reported about $423M in 2025 revenue within a direct prop-firm market Octrado estimates at $4.0–4.5B a year. Traditional firms set opaque house rules and retain evaluation fees for shareholders; Vanta pitches public, rule-based scoring paired with fee-funded burns that benefit SN8 holders.
SN8

Vanta

Trading · prop-trading network
5,880Cumulative trader accounts · Nov 26
$354KLifetime buyback wallet inflows · Nov 26
Response to the 2026 rules

When eTAO went live, Vanta founder Arrash Yasavolian set SN8’s split on October 20 to 0% owner, 50% validator and 50% miner, paired with a July 16 Kraken listing and our cohort’s largest conviction lock at 35.6% of eligible alpha, with 35.4% locked by the owner’s own wallet.

Cutting the owner share does not mean Taoshi takes no emissions: Arrash openly stated that the team funds operations via staking yield and self-mining through Vanta Trading, earning alpha in proportion to PnL. That is more transparent than hidden self-mining, but means Vanta’s 0% owner cut cannot be read without checking who captures the 50% miner bucket.

“We believe removing owner emissions is part of a subnet’s maturation. Once you’ve built a stable & fair incentive mechanism, you can compete within it yourself... APY from our existing holdings will fund subnet features and improvements. We’ll rely on mining emissions and Vanta Trading’s ability to compete to fund our continued growth.”

Arrash Yasavolian · Founder, Vanta / Taoshi · X, Oct 20, 2026
How value reaches alpha

Vanta’s token flows span three different public views, leaving the net customer-funded share open:

  • Dedicated buyback wallet: On vantanetwork.io/metrics, Vanta reports $353,505 in lifetime inflows, deploying 46,237 alpha as of November 26.
  • Mixed-source emission coverage: Its tokenomics dashboard shows 69.8% of November miner emissions covered, following a team-reported 72% in October. Because Vanta combines evaluation fees, forfeited collateral, prior-month balances, conviction locks and unclaimed emissions into one total without disclosing dollar fee revenue, outside customer cash cannot be isolated.
  • All-wallet on-chain perimeter: SubConnect’s tracker ranks Vanta #2 in November at $514.7K and #1 in consistency at $1.41M across 11 of 12 months. Yet 64% of November’s total, or $331.1K, sits in provisional Tier 4 burns with no matching purchase, versus 12% Tier 1, 14% Tier 2 and 9% Tier 3.

Next, Vanta plans to replace upfront registration fees with permissionless, collateral-based registration, targeted for the first week of December.

Risk Factors
  • Self-mining and entity concentration. Even when openly disclosed, critics flag the structural tension when an operator sets scoring rules while competing as the flagship entity miner. On Vanta’s live dashboard, 547 of 659 active traders, or 83%, sit inside entity subaccounts, and two parent entity hotkeys hold 81.2% of active accounts at 65.3% and 15.9%. Because parent hotkeys and per-entity emission shares are unlabeled, outsiders cannot verify how much of the 50% miner bucket goes to Taoshi versus independent miners.
  • Opaque burn attribution and circular-flow questions. With 64% of Vanta’s November buybacks, or $331.1K, classified as provisional Tier 4 burns without a matched purchase on SubConnect’s tracker, and without total dollar fee disclosures separating customer cash from forfeited collateral, prior-month balances and unclaimed emissions, holders cannot separate net external cash from protocol loops.
  • Simulated scoring and prop-firm risks. All SN8 scoring runs in simulation against live price feeds (the dashboard explicitly notes "Simulated performance, not payouts"), leaving open how much live-capital yield exists relative to evaluation fees and emissions. Independent miners also cite harsh drawdown penalties and sudden rule updates, alongside regulatory scrutiny and December’s untested collateral-registration shift.
Takeaway

Vanta reports combined burns and locks covering 69.8% of November miner emissions alongside the network’s longest on-chain buyback streak and largest owner lock. Until it breaks out external customer fees from forfeited collateral, unclaimed emissions and the 64% of November buybacks sitting in Tier 4 burn-only, the net customer-funded share remains open.

What to prove next

Publish evaluation revenue and a recurring burn breakdown: customer fees, forfeited collateral and unclaimed emissions.

2.5 Compute and inference: where the revenue sits

Before the top rung of our ladder, compute sets the macro backdrop. Unlike drug discovery or prop evaluations, GPU rental and model inference already have liquid buyer demand, accounting for 78–82% of SubConnect’s estimated subnet revenue.

High top-line compute revenue still does not establish standalone profitability. Costs and margins are undisclosed, and commodity GPU or inference providers can lean on emissions to stay price-competitive, whereas application subnets aim to sell the same workflow repeatedly once demand scales.

Lium reported $2.32M in October renter spending. Its published 5% platform fee implies about $116K in fees that month. The distinction matters when comparing a rental marketplace with a provider that bills customers directly.

Targon reported burning 8,450 TAO of SN4 alpha in the final week of October, attributing 1,772 TAO to organic revenue. Live data on bittensorrevenueindex.com shows how lumpy compute buybacks remain: Lium drove $3.08M in November on its own, while Targon and Chutes both logged $0 through November 26 despite $1.94M and $3.11M over the past 12 months.

Chutes offers a third lens on compute economics because its API revenue and pool issuance can be compared over nearly matched dates.

As detailed in The Lium question in Section 01, Lium’s $3.08M November buyback surge still exceeds a full year of implied 5% platform fees and cannot yet be assumed as steady-state cash flow without an audit.

Issuance against revenue at Chutes (SN64)

Over the August–September period shown, Bittensor issued about $7 worth of TAO to Chutes’ pool for every $1 Chutes earned in estimated revenue, using the average daily on-chain emission share for the period (see Method notes). A second tracker records about half that share, which gives roughly $4. Either way, issuance was several times revenue. Chutes’ costs are unknown.

Monthly revenue fell between our two reports: DefiLlama tracked about $464K in February 2026 and $388K in August, and its Chutes revenue series still ended on September 6 when re-checked on November 26.

How Chutes is trying to grow paid usage

Chutes started by cutting free and unprofitable usage, tightening subscriptions and putting more emphasis on pay-as-you-go customers. It has since widened distribution and added models. SayGM began offering Chutes models in October. In November, Chutes added Tencent’s Hy4 model to its API, and Chutes announced a partnership with Alibaba Cloud to expand its model lineup.

These launches give developers more ways to use Chutes. The revenue figures above predate them, so their effect on paid usage is still open.

Rung 5 of 5 · Clean customer-funded burnsAt the top of the ladder sits Engy, the only profiled subnet where billed developer usage converts directly into documented, 100% Tier 1 on-chain token burns.

Low prices can bring customers to an inference subnet; reliability, privacy and verification give them reasons to stay. Where Chutes illustrates the scale of the subsidy gap in open inference, Engy tests whether tying miner scoring and alpha burns directly to paid API traffic can narrow it.

What Engy is building

Engy, built by Hanlin AI, lets developers buy open-weight LLM inference from independent GPU operators through a single OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible API. A team running a coding agent or support assistant can pick an open model, route calls through Engy and pay per token without rewriting its client stack.

As open-weight models narrow the gap with closed labs, cheap API buyers still worry about silent quantization or model substitution. Centralized hosts like Together AI offer mature serverless deployments on the same models, asking customers to trust their infrastructure.

Engy replaces that trust assumption with optional cryptographic checks: weights are pinned to a published hash, miners attach compact activation fingerprints (TOPLOC) to responses, and sampled recompute audits verify the exact checkpoint served. Full verification still requires model-grade hardware, and the audit verifier is still rolling out.

Usage growth and miner incentives

SubConnect named Engy among the drivers of network revenue growth. On Engy’s usage dashboard, traffic reached 3.72T tokens over the past 30 closed days across nine active models, averaging 124B tokens a day after peaking at 192B on November 18, led by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro.

Under Engy’s active scoring rule, miners earn rewards strictly on successful billed tokens, tying operator payouts to live customer traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks.

That direct link is set to soften. Engy merged PR #62 into its main branch on November 16, documenting a planned shift to an 80% baseline uptime pool and 20% paid-traffic split, though 100% of emissions still follow paid traffic until the team sets a cutover epoch. Rewarding availability helps keep spare GPU capacity ready for burst demand, but it also pulls subnet incentives back toward subsidizing idle supply rather than rewarding billed usage alone.

Response to the 2026 rules

Engy’s revenue-funded buyback and burn went live on August 12, about two weeks after the Emission Gate, though no causal link between the two is documented. Engy enabled Gamma on November 10 and rolled out accountless hotkey deposits on November 22; by November 26, SubnetRadar logged $572 minted and $319 spent across 15 deposits and 8 coldkeys (still modest next to its existing buyback ledger, and worth tracking separately for repeat commercial demand).

How value reaches alpha

Engy’s public buyback ledger records customer API revenue buying TAO and then SN53 alpha for permanent burn, totaling 59,071 alpha, or $440.6K at transaction values, across 28 burns through November 21. Independent tracking on bittensorrevenueindex.com corroborates that record, ranking Engy #3 network-wide in November at $186.6K in buybacks, 100% classified as Tier 1 bought-and-burned, and $441.5K over 12 months.

Among our five profiles, that gives Engy the cleanest documented bridge from paid usage to token burns. Still, Table 10 keeps the scale in perspective: at its 4.34% emission share on November 26, Bittensor is injecting roughly $10.5M a year of TAO into Engy’s pool, far above cumulative burns to date, and conviction locks remain small at 4.0% combined, with 3.7% owner-locked.

Risk Factors
  • Pricing and model mix. Engy cut prices by about 30% in October, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which carried 83% of trailing 30-day token volume, doubled in price on Nov 20. Over more recent days, Kimi K3.1 Pro ramped to ~26% of daily tokens after launching Nov 4, measured over that shorter recent window rather than summing with DeepSeek’s 30-day share. How customers respond to those prices sets Engy’s burn capacity.
  • Reporting. The burns are visible on-chain; that customer revenue funds them is team-attributed and unaudited.
  • Holder concentration. Subnet Summer flags that a large share of Engy alpha sits in a single non-owner wallet; a large sale could move price sharply.
Takeaway

Engy shows how paid inference can fund alpha buybacks and burns. Its next test is whether customers keep spending as prices and miner incentives change.

What to prove next

Disclose monthly paid usage, revenue, and attributable burns post-Nov 20; report Gamma spending separately.

2.7 What the profiles add up to

Read together from Carbon up to Engy, the five profiles form a commercial ladder: Carbon and Metanova are proving research workflows ahead of revenue, REAX has paying users without a token buyback yet, Vanta runs recurring buybacks without isolating customer fees, and Engy turns billed developer traffic cleanly into 100% Tier 1 burns.

Even so, commercial traction, customer-funded token purchases and verified owner locks remain separate achievements, and no single subnet yet combines all three with full disclosure.

What do these purchases mean for token holders?

Pool depth limits what a buyback does to price. Daily protocol liquidity makes the largest pools unusually deep: at the Exploit convention, Yuma noted that top pools carry too much liquidity relative to trading volume, and TAO Daily observed that a 1,000 $TAO sell on Chutes moves its price by roughly 1%. The depth that absorbs sales also absorbs purchases, while thin long-tail pools move sharply both ways.

“Market discussions often start with the assumption that more liquidity is better. Yuma’s research, recently presented at @Exploitsummit, demonstrates how excess liquidity can suppress price discovery, obscuring quality and risk information from capital allocators.”

Yuma · ASMR Research Preview · X, Oct 12, 2026

Two proposals target pool depth: Yuma’s ASMR proposal would recycle liquidity out of pools, and Bittensor’s planned lending and borrowing upgrade, which Const described as directionally aligned with ASMR, would change borrowing mechanics. Neither has shipped yet.

Do verified buybacks show up in price?

Table 10 shows the customer money we can see coming back to alpha. A separate question is whether those purchases show up in price. In a co-author study shown in Figure 6 and Table 11, Subnet Summer tracked all 10 subnets with verified on-chain buyback wallets from Sep 1 to Nov 22 against an 88-subnet control group holding at least 2,000 $TAO on Sep 1.

Subnets with verified on-chain buybacks returned a median +14.5% against $TAO from September 1 to November 22, a 39.5-point spread over the −25% median across 88 control subnets, with daily pool volume rising for six of the 10 while falling 32% among the rest.

Buybacks were not the only driver: team share of buying, volume, emission changes and pool depth also mattered, and 10 names is too small a sample to establish causation.

How teams responded to the 2026 rules

Beyond token purchases, the clearest documented responses to the new rules concern how teams allocate rewards. Vanta set its owner share to 0% (while transparently self-mining through its flagship entity miner), REAX reported 26%, and Metanova planned a 26% owner share to fund experimental data. Metanova also publicly linked its June 24 cut to miner burn to the new incentives.

Engy’s revenue-funded burns began about two weeks after the Emission Gate, and SubConnect counted 14 subnets funding buybacks by August 26. Neither source establishes that the gate caused those decisions. Changes to reward settings and payment mechanisms are documented. Their effect on customer growth remains uncertain.

2.8 Who has locked their tokens?

Conviction locks became a confidence signal after July’s upgrade and Covenant AI’s April exit. Ownership can transfer only after a subnet turns a year old and only if a single hotkey exceeds 18% of eligible alpha.

Because conviction builds over time, new locks carry less weight than mature ones. Across all 113 locked subnets tracked on November 26, zero challengers had cleared the 18% gate.

What the breakdown shows is commitment. Alpha locked directly from the owner’s wallet ties up the team’s own tokens. A lock directed to the owner’s hotkey from an outside wallet says more about holder confidence than the team’s unless the team confirms custody, and it does not stop an owner from selling.

Other subnets to watch: Niome, Minos, Hippius, SayGM and RedTeam
03 · Catalysts & Risk Factors

What 2027 has to show

In short. Four signals would show customer demand catching up with issuance in 2027: comparable revenue growth, repeat use, documented token purchases and independent research validation.

Into 2027

Can customer revenue catch up with issuance?

Signs of progress
  1. Comparable growth. SubConnect reports higher revenue across the same set of subnets.
  2. Repeat use. Unaffiliated customers come back to pay for the same subnet services, including through Gamma credits.
  3. Documented token purchases. More subnets show customer revenue funding buybacks, with the customer share broken out.
  4. Independent validation. Research subnets clear milestones partners can reproduce, such as Metanova’s in-vitro results.
Risks to watch
  1. Customer revenue grows more slowly than the dollar value of TAO issuance.
  2. Concentration: revenue stays in compute, where inference is crowded.
  3. Governance: Root Reborn and Null Consensus put allocation and scoring in fewer hands.
  4. Builder exit: teams below the bar have less reason to stay.
  5. Liquidity: deep top pools mute the price impact of buybacks, while thin long-tail pools amplify exits.
What would change our mind
  • The revenue index flattens or falls over the next two readings.
  • Issuance per dollar of revenue rises on matched periods while the $TAO price holds.
  • No non-compute subnet discloses repeat revenue from unaffiliated customers in 2027 (token link tracked separately).

Khala Research and Subnet Summer analysis.

04 · Closing Thesis

Customers are arriving. Now the trend has to compound.

In February, The Intelligence Olympics closed with one open question: how much of the market could Bittensor’s subnets capture? Nine months later, there are numbers to answer with.

Estimated revenue roughly doubled to ~$70M in three months, a meaningful step up from earlier in the year and an encouraging sign if that pace holds. A real gap still separates customer spend from issuance: buyers pay roughly $1 for every $3.50 of new TAO issued at November prices, and outside Lium, matched on-chain buybacks hold near 5% of minted TAO.

Even February’s two clearest token-value links showed how fragile early routes remain: Templar’s fee-to-buyback model left the network when Covenant AI exited on April 9, and Chutes logged $0 in on-chain buybacks through November 26 despite leading early inference revenue.

Still, the rules now point the right way. Emissions follow sustained token demand, owners can pledge their own share, and customers can pay through Gamma in a way that burns supply at the point of sale. Across our five-rung ladder, concrete proof points are emerging:

  • Research pipelines live: Carbon launched its hidden-data validation mainnet, and Metanova sent 50 nanobody candidates toward lab testing.
  • Early paid adoption: REAX debuted at #1 on Hugging Face’s Decision Index weeks after launch and began billing API users.
  • Recurring buybacks and owner skin in the game: Vanta logged 11 straight months of on-chain buybacks alongside a 35.6% conviction lock.
  • Clean customer-funded burns: Engy turned 3.72T tokens of paid developer inference into 100% Tier 1 on-chain burns.

2027 decides whether builders use that runway once the market demands revenue alongside emissions. Watch three things in the next edition of this report:

  • The Lium question: whether November’s surge proves to be Lium’s alone, or whether reconciled, multi-subnet buybacks finally lift the network cleanly above its ~5% matched baseline.
  • A second clean burner: whether another high-volume subnet joins Engy in pairing disclosed commercial usage with 100% Tier 1 token burns.
  • A paying research partner: whether Metanova or Carbon converts open miner competitions into an external pharma licensing deal or paid industrial audit.

Method and Data Notes

Snapshot dates and cutoff. Editorial cutoff is November 26, 2026 (live on-chain and dashboard snapshots pulled around 02:00–02:45 UTC on November 26, 2026). Individual status checks and snapshots are dated where they appear; protocol dates are month-level unless a specific activation date is cited.

Chutes issuance and revenue. 11.3% average daily share of network emission, Aug 10 to Sep 6, 2026 (bittensor.ai daily series) × ~3,600 $TAO/day × 365 × $218.2 average $TAO price (CoinGecko) ≈ $32.4M. Revenue: Chutes API via DefiLlama, annualized through Sep 6. Sensitivity at the same historical revenue run rate: 7.94% (bittensor.ai, Nov 26, 2026) × $185 ≈ $19.3M (~4.3:1). Second tracker: Own Your Mind's chain index shows Chutes at 6.55% on Aug 15 and 5.82% on Sep 22, 2026, roughly half the bittensor.ai series; 6.55% gives ≈ $18.8M, or ~4.1:1. The trackers give different emission shares. The revenue window starts two days before the issuance window.

Five kinds of revenue and inflow figure, never added together.

  • Monthly index estimate: SubConnect's monthly annualized revenue estimate, used for the network total, trend and compute's share. Per SubConnect (private call with Khala, Nov 24, 2026), the index is compiled monthly from direct team check-ins (roughly 80–90% of covered subnets) combined with public dashboards and on-chain data where available (such as Lium and Engy). It annualizes trailing monthly or hourly run rates as annualized revenue rather than contracted ARR, and excludes non-revenue deposits. The early-October ($50M+) reading leaned more heavily on extrapolation, while the November 4 (~$70M) reading followed direct team check-ins. "Verified" is SubConnect's term, as reported by TokenPost; no written methodology has been published yet for the monthly team check-in index.
  • Live on-chain buyback and fee tracker: SubConnect's newly launched dashboard (bittensorrevenueindex.com, counted hourly from Taostats data across 128 subnets; written counting rules at /methodology). Measures on-chain alpha buybacks across four evidence tiers, Gamma mints and miner registration fees, excluding protocol chain buys. Annualizes the last 30 whole days × 12; includes Tier 4 provisional burn-only in headline ARR by default while excluding it from P&L "Money in." Formal off-chain audits (/audits) are not open yet ("None yet").
  • Company-reported, read by a tracker: Chutes' revenue API via DefiLlama's adapter, a 30-day window, annualized. The endpoint now requires authentication.
  • Company-reported: October renter spend and published fee terms for Lium, plus dated figures from Engy, Vanta, Metanova and REAX.
  • Other third-party: BlockEden, context only.

Khala calculations compare issuance value with revenue, not costs or profit. Chutes’ ratio is ~7.1:1 using bittensor.ai (~4.1:1 on the alternative tracker) over near-matched Aug–Sep windows. At the network level, gross TAO issuance is ~3.5:1 at $185/TAO on November 26 (~$243M/yr, or ~3.7:1 at $195/TAO), while sellable alpha emissions are ~7.6:1 on Subnet Summer’s November 16 snapshot ($195/TAO and 1.219 sum of subnet prices, ~$535M/yr) or ~6.7:1 (~$468M/yr) repriced to November 26’s $185/TAO and 1.123 sum of subnet prices (emitted alpha is not necessarily sold).

Sellable alpha emissions. Subnet Summer’s Nov 16 on-chain snapshot: sellable alpha per subnet per day × sum of subnet prices in TAO (1.219) × $195 per TAO × 365, net of conviction-locked alpha ≈ $535M. The total implies about 6,170 sellable alpha per subnet per day after the lock deduction. The figure assumes every subnet emits alpha at the same rate and treats all unlocked alpha as sellable; it does not measure actual selling.

At $185/TAO (Nov 26, taostats.io / bittensor.ai), after the next halving (~1,800 $TAO/day, estimated Dec 12, 2029 on taostats), gross protocol issuance would annualize to ~$122M. bittensor.ai

Not measured: subnet costs, margins, outside-customer share, causal burn effects on prices (Table 11 tracks observed Sep 1 to Nov 22 returns, not causation), or revenue outside SubConnect’s coverage. Chutes’ revenue series ends September 6; daily concentration data begins after the Emission Gate launch.

On-chain minted TAO denominator (Figure 3 & Box 1). On bittensorrevenueindex.com, November’s 83,840 TAO minted covers Nov 1 through Nov 26 at 07:07 UTC (~25.3 days, averaging ~3,314 net TAO/day vs. the ~3,600 TAO/day nominal 12-second schedule, and excluding anomalous supply-adjustment days on May 28 and Sep 15). Minor Gamma dollar differences between SubnetRadar ($104.0K total, $80.3K Lium) and SubConnect ($103.9K total, $80.1K Lium) reflect hourly TAO-price valuation and cutoff timing.

Buyback study (Table 11 & Figure 6, co-author analysis by Subnet Summer). Covers Sep 1 to Nov 22, 2026. The 10-subnet buyback cohort includes subnets with verified on-chain team buyback wallets tracked via TaoMarketCap (a stricter on-chain sample than the 14 subnets SubConnect cited in August); ReadyAI had 0 Chain TAO during the window, SayGM team TAO is a minimum due to customer-paid burns, and Score buybacks began ~Nov 9. Chain TAO is modeled from Subtensor’s SubnetExcessTao via Taosis daily closes; Team share = Team TAO ÷ (Chain TAO + Team TAO). The 88-subnet control group consists of non-buyback subnets with a Sep 1 pool of at least 2,000 TAO. Small sample (n = 10); shows observed returns, not causation.

Selection. Hand-picked, not a sample.
